reference.reference_reason: Both identify kidnapping. Local derivational records do not provide a complete cross-language history.
Both identify botulism; Danish explicitly borrows the German term. This is borrowing rather than uninterrupted native cognacy.
Cup/goblet vessels overlap, but the chosen German cup/trophy sense differs from a generic Danish cup. Danish calyx/dicebox uses are also additional.
Fake/feign overlaps, while Danish copy/imitate can also be non-deceptive. Different compositional bases do not establish a connected history here.
Obvious/evident and overt/manifest overlap explicitly. Apparent must refer to evident rather than merely seeming; German history is absent.
Both identify aardvark with explicit Dutch/Afrikaans calque history. Matching conceptual construction need not mean all morphemes are inherited equivalents.
A fact and reality are related abstractions but not generally interchangeable nouns; these entries do not record a common exact sense.
Both mean criterion and record Greek kriterion, German via Latin.
Pedantic and finical can overlap in excessive fussiness, but affected/hoity-toity is not general pedantry. Sources do not establish shared history.
Living together is a form of coexistence, while coexistence can be broader. Local formations do not supply a common historical path.
Both identify Sunday and explicitly record the sun-day calque family. German municipality and historical place-name entries are separate.
False/untrue overlaps explicitly, while German wrong/fake/immoral/perfidious meanings are additional. Different recorded sources do not prove full unrelatedness.
Both record omen, while Danish notice/warning and German technical sign uses differ. Their recorded derivations do not establish whole-word unrelatedness.
Danish gene is not German directional gen, which is dated/inactive. Danish explicitly borrows capitalized German Gen, a different noun entry from gen.
Target only redirects to the former spelling Maß; its underlying senses must be resolved before comparison with Danish buttocks.
Danish mood/caprice derives through Latin luna, while German Luna names the Roman deity or a given name. Shared lunar source does not establish present equivalence; warm is another Danish entry.
Pulsation and powdery have distinct meanings and grammatical roles. Their common prefix spelling is insufficient.
Both record elf/fairy senses and Germanic albiz. English fantasy-race, fish, and Christmas uses are not all Danish counterparts; the male name is separate.
The adverb differently coincides explicitly. Danish also has an adjective different; grammatical identity must refer to the chosen adverb entry.
Danish explicitly borrows English brunch. Meal meaning is shared; direct borrowing differs from uninterrupted inherited cognacy.
Both have connection meanings. The selected English buses/systems sense is restricted; multiple other English meanings are not translations of forbindelse.
The strict English preposition sense matches Danish. The selected English broad adposition sense is wider and includes other positional classes.
Both are pedestrian bridges. Recorded decompositions differ: walking+bridge versus foot+bridge; shared whole-compound inheritance is not established.
Both identify the Norse giant category with recorded etunaz history. English is a learned Norse borrowing, not uninterrupted native descent.
Cookie/cracker overlaps the listed British and other regional biscuit meanings. American soft bread and technical/slang senses do not all match. Danish borrows cakes, not the English biscuit form.

The selected English verb concerns a client action, not a prostituted person. Saved English senses omit the ordinary sex-worker noun; this omission should not be mistaken for proof of no real noun overlap.
The building-room nouns explicitly coincide and share ruman history. Space, compartment, verb, nautical and archaic adjectival uses need separate treatment.
The thatching verbs share explicit takjanan ancestry and reciprocal cognate mentions. Roof-covering nouns and Danish charm entry must remain separate.
Both record Latin mysterium, but English has only historical/inactive substance or radio-source senses here. Those do not match the Danish ordinary mystery headline.
Both identify ytterbium and explicitly form it from Ytterby plus element suffix. Same element/source-name construction is useful equivalence, not uninterrupted native inherited vocabulary.

Animal anus/scupper and gate/barrier openings are not exact translations in the saved senses despite common gata ancestry. Other English technical openings do not establish a Danish scupper counterpart here.
Livestock and an unspecified surname have no observed common concept or identity.
Both ultimately record Greek margaron, but a spread and a pearl-related/acid adjective differ. Shared source history is not shared current meaning.
Both are female given names; this is not identity. French/Latin versus Selene/Greek routes are recorded, without complete family resolution.
Generic surname definitions do not establish Seefeld/Seefeldt as variants or identify the same people. Danish named biographies do not resolve the English surname.
The Danish discursive gloss supports overlap but leaves which English discourse/digression/reasoning senses apply unresolved. A full Danish borrowing path is absent.
Teacher and underside have no observed shared meaning. Similar under-components do not make the complete words cognates or translations.
Related is an adjective; a relative is a person. The similar family stems suggest a derivational relationship but the records do not provide its complete path.
Both explicitly record the penalty fine sense and botō history. Selected fine versus remedy misses that shared meaning; Danish booth is another historical entry.
Donation coincides explicitly. Latin history is recorded only in Norwegian, so full Danish shared-source transmission remains inferred.
Both identify alder and record common aluz ancestry and cross-references. Danish electricity is another entry; short-form filtering would lose a valid tree word.
Fat/obese coincides explicitly. Danish fatty/cool/bold and homographic nouns, and Norwegian thick, are additional uses; different immediate roots do not independently prove unrelatedness.
Both mean goose and record Old Norse gas and Proto-Germanic gans.
A requirement overlaps need/requirement, but demand and need are not equivalent in all contexts. Different recorded historical paths do not alone prove unrelatedness.
Horny/frisky overlaps explicitly. Exuberance, health and cocktail uses differ. Danish kanhtaz versus Norwegian karskr is incomplete evidence for their full historical relation.
Companion and a business partner can overlap situationally, but these bare glosses do not establish a general interchangeable sense.
Without versus than/yet/and do not overlap in the supplied senses. Distinct recorded roots alone do not prove independent origin.
Both mean knead, with Norwegian specifying dough. Recorded Norse elta and knoda are different immediate sources, not independently proven unrelated roots. Danish mud is another grammatical entry.
Norwegian drown is explicitly derived from remain-at-sea with the same historical blive source. The Danish passive auxiliary, become, and remain senses do not mean drown.
Both identify the Greek Titan Iapetus, with matching Greek source and Norwegian disambiguation distinguishing moon and ocean name forms.
Both identify cholesterol. Greek components are recorded only in Norwegian, so the full common-source path on Danish remains inferred.
Sending is an action; a sender is its agent. The form relationship is a reasonable derivational inference, not a documented complete ancestry path here.
Both record Latin spectaculum history, but Danish disturbance/noise and Norwegian spectacular adjective differ in present meaning and grammar.
Tray, hill, tool jaw, and backing are not a tailgate. Possible back-component resemblance concerns one historical entry, not the selected tray or the complete compound.
A traveller is an agent, while travel/voyage is an action; both selected glosses are archaic/inactive. Norwegian also has active travel verbs and a separate danger entry.

Norwegian explicitly borrows Danish Berthel and identifies it as a spelling variant of Bertel. This is supported name-family correspondence, not merely generic male-name gloss similarity or same-person identity.
Leap year and shoulder name different concepts. Similar short spellings provide no shared sense.
Summerhouse and butterfly differ. The shared summer component does not establish full-compound equivalence or ancestry.
A confirmand is a participant; confirming is an action. Related religious domain and similar forms do not make noun and verb equivalent.
Both record kidnapping, with different morphological bases. Their histories are not connected by these local derivation records.
Both record alder and aluz ancestry. Two-letter forms can be valid cognates; Danish electricity is another entry.
Confectionery and candy overlap in ordinary use. The Swedish entry has no historical record here; common history is not established.
Subdue explicitly overlaps. Danish Norse kuga is stated, while Swedish marks the Danish/Norse source as only possible and offers an alternative; retain that uncertainty.
Suspect and think-that-something-is-true can overlap in uncertain belief, while trusting a person can contrast with suspicion. The selected trust sense misses that contextual overlap.
Suspicious and distrustful overlap. Different bases for suspect and trust plus a negative prefix do not establish whole-word cognacy.
Both record an organized procession. Swedish paired/mated adjectival entries are homographs, not the selected parade sense.
Scuffle/brawl and uproar/racket overlap, while Swedish fraction is a different use. Danish Latin history does not establish Swedish ancestry.
Both record Norse vindauga, but Swedish window is archaic/inactive; selected wind-source horizon point is not a window.
Both record rabid with the same German and Latin borrowing chain. Danish fanatic/brutal/coarse expansions require separate coverage checks.
Wrong-word/Freudian-slip and hurrying/running-fast meanings differ. A foreword noun is another Danish entry.
To apply and applied are verb versus adjective/participle. Danish Latin history and form resemblance support a family inference, not exact grammatical equivalence.
Give birth versus born are active verb and adjectival/participle meanings. Danish feeding and food senses are additional; Swedish full history is absent.
Logic versus lodging have distinct supplied meanings despite close spelling.
Danish explicitly calls Jorgine a feminine form of Jorgen; Swedish Jorgen borrows that Danish male name. The variants are related but are not interchangeable names of one person.
Support/base/surface underneath and underdog do not share a recorded meaning. The under-like component alone is insufficient.
Both mean misleading. Swedish records mis-plus-showing composition; Danish history is absent, so matching morphology supplies an inference rather than recorded ancestry.
The financial budget meaning coincides. German explicitly borrows via French from English; old English bag and other senses should not dominate the comparison.
Both identify Thursday with recorded thunder-god-day source and reciprocal comparison. English adverb on-Thursday is a separate grammatical use.
Both identify yew plants with explicit common ancestry and a cognate statement. English wood, bow, and dialectal-you senses are additional uses.
Both record wedge. English shim also has thin alignment material, software, and other senses; its physical-word origin is explicitly unknown.
Both mean maize/corn, German regionally marked. Serbo-Croatian/Romanian versus Taino source paths do not by themselves prove completely unrelated ancestry.
Mixed cold dish and greens senses overlap with explicit Italian/French borrowing family. German Islamic prayer is another historical entry, not a salad meaning.
Decay/deterioration overlaps the state of dilapidation. German general decline/decadence and English building damage/payment usages are not wholly equivalent.
English occasional/incidental overlaps the German gloss. Happening by chance is related but not the same as occurring incidentally; informal/relaxed meanings are additional English uses.

The shared weaning sense is present and ancestry is recorded. The selected English intransitive cease-to-depend gloss omits the transitive ordinary weaning counterpart; the child noun is another entry.
Against/opposition overlaps explicitly with recorded gagin ancestry and a cognate statement; other directional, approximate, and grammatical uses do not all coincide.
Weak can overlap not-strong flavor or intensity in mild, but not-serious/dangerous is not a general translation of weak. Distinct recorded roots alone do not establish unrelatedness.
The sowing verbs share recorded Germanic ancestry and meaning. English female-animal and surname homographs must remain separate.
The selected Austrian town is explicitly the same in both; German also has several river senses.

The sources connect sorrel-related old forms through Germanic ampraz, but current English tumour/flaw glosses omit the German plant meaning. Shared ancestry is separate from current semantic disjointness in these entries.
Both record Latin femina, but female committee and female-ostrich feather are not equivalent meanings.
A manuscript copy and pertaining to that copy are noun versus adjective. English fine-grained is another meaning; Greek history is recorded only for the German noun.

The glosses describe related signaling-protein concepts but do not establish whether chemerin is a chemokine or an interchangeable term. A biochemical source check is needed; shared chemo-like form is insufficient.
Latin apostrophus is shared, and the English apostrophe-symbol sense is archaic/inactive. The selected active reverse-C numeral sign is not German inverted comma.
Chromatin and chrismation are distinct scientific and religious concepts. Greek colour versus chrism-related derivation does not establish complete historical unrelatedness.
A Latin-derived given name and an unspecified surname do not identify matching entities or documented name variants.
An idea/message and the Greek city Messene are different concepts. German borrowing from English message does not link it to Messene.
A town/village name and a surname from German are not matching identities. Flat tire is another German entry.
Both generic surname glosses do not establish the same name. German also has the electrical unit, omitted from the selected display.
Rendering and tapestry repair are not the same action; renters of property are also unrelated to rendering. German borrows render, not renter.
The two systematic element names are different, and the English entry is marked dated/inactive. Its hypothetical active equivalence must not be manufactured from their shared element-name pattern.
Performance can overlap rendition, but the generic glosses do not settle scope; NAOB supplies representation/reproduction evidence, not complete equivalence.
Both record the thrown discus object, but the selected Norwegian sport/action is not the object. Latin and Greek sources suggest a borrowing family without a full linking path in these entries.

Both record Old Norse jarl; the selected German Norse title and active Norwegian British earl use are different institutional titles. The matching Norse-title Norwegian sense is marked historical/inactive.
Both mean method and record Latin methodus from Greek methodos.
The district sense overlaps, with German marked especially Switzerland. German accommodation and Norwegian quarter-hour/moon uses do not coincide. Both record French quartier.
German is only a spelling redirect to einschließen. Resolve the referenced lemma before deciding whether enclosure/including overlaps append; a redirect gloss is not a meaning.
Both mean bulletproof. Recorded shot-plus-firm/secure composition supports structural analogy; common ancestry of both complete compounds is not established.
Disguising/clouding can hide information, overlapping conceal/hide. Literal veiling and physical hiding are not interchangeable in every context; history is not established.

German Jupiter includes astronomical and Roman-tagged entries; Norwegian disambiguates planet and deity and adds distinct places. The planet sense is shared; same spelling must not collapse all place names.
German pure and Norwegian only/merely may overlap in restrictive constructions; bare versus but is not a shared headline. A related derivation is plausible but not documented in Norwegian here.
Recorded malmaz history connects the forms, but tooth-grinding action and conifer heartwood differ in meaning and part of speech.
Northeast and north coast differ. A north component can relate while the complete concepts and second components differ.
A synapse and poorly informed opinion-giving name different concepts and parts of speech. The Norwegian derivation does not supply German historical evidence.
Israelite and a modern Israeli citizen refer to distinct categories despite the recorded Israel base. Same demonym-like form does not settle identity.
An initiator is an agent; initiative is an act or disposition. Shared activity does not make these nouns equivalent.
Elf/fairy overlap is explicit with common albiz ancestry, but German especially-evil chest-sitter and Swedish female mythological creature are not complete cultural equivalents.

The mythological creatures overlap, with Swedish specifying a female fairy/elf. German elf is borrowed from English while Swedish inherits the Germanic family; German eleven/team meanings are separate.
Both record political hawk/hard-liner senses. Selected falcon versus hawk bird meanings differ; historical root strings also differ without independently proving unrelatedness.
Wrinkle is shared; German also has fold and Swedish has verb/fabric uses. Whole histories remain unresolved.
Precious-metal fineness coincides explicitly, Swedish rare but active. Its historical silver restriction and figurative quality sense are separately recorded.
Stalk and straw/haulm overlap as plant-stem material with common halmaz ancestry, but generic stalk includes growing stems and straw is a more specific material/use.
Both identify insulated coolboxes and record cooling-plus-box composition. Complete cross-language historical paths are inferred rather than documented here.
A string-instrument nut and a bolt nut are different objects. Their shared English translation word is a polysemy trap, not evidence that the source words share that sense.
Extremely and abundantly/heavily can both express degree but do not generally modify the same predicates. The bare glosses cannot establish a common interchangeable sense.
The bully meaning coincides, but German is dated/inactive. A valid historical overlap must be distinguished from a suitable modern active headline.
Cheating is shared, but German also has dizziness and harmless lying; separate recorded derivations do not prove unrelatedness.

The saved German gloss only records reciprocal each-other, not the Swedish reflexive headline. German native-edition definitions and Swedish sig translations confirm omitted ordinary reflexive overlap; common sek ancestry is recorded.
Injury or violation of rules is not invasion. These saved senses offer no mutual translation, although invasion can cause injury or violate rules.

Saved German some and Swedish exclamatory what-a do not match. Native German source records interrogative/relative welcher with welche inflections and Swedish vilken translation, establishing omitted ordinary which correspondence.
Fearful/anxious and timid overlap in a fearful disposition, but anxiety need not imply timidity. Swedish history is absent.
The sources share puttaz history, but Swedish pot/kitty is not disambiguated as a cooking vessel. German bare pot also needs resolution before claiming a common current sense.
The named Bonn hill/quarter and anatomical mons veneris are different referents even with an explicitly shared Latin calque.
Mild/gentle and rope/wire/line differ in grammar and meaning; the Swedish given name is another entry. Distinct immediate roots do not prove full unrelatedness.
Stem/stalk/handle meanings do not match the Swedish still adverb. Similar spelling is not meaning overlap.
Helix and holy do not overlap in these senses. A Swedish Germanic root does not establish the German noun ancestry.
Both record textile fringe; the chosen eyelash misses that shared sense. The Swedish male-name history belongs to another entry and does not supply fringe ancestry.
Different male/female given-name descriptions do not establish equivalent name variants or a shared history.
A Ukrainian person and Ukrainian as a relational adjective concern the same country but have distinct grammar and meanings.
A mineral and a male given name are different concepts. The shared Alexander-like form does not establish a historical path in these records.
Both are formed from Mauritius, but Mauritian as a relational adjective and a Mauritian person are distinct grammatical meanings.
Planning/agenda is shared and both record Latin agenda; English also has planner and ulterior-motive senses.
Blunt edge/adjective meanings differ from stub/fragments, buttocks and children. A cigar versus its butt is likewise not the same sense.
Both record chaos with Greek khaos history. English mathematical, cosmological and named-entity senses need separate alignments.
Both explicitly record chili. The Norwegian bare gloss does not establish every English pepper/powder/dish correspondence; shared borrowing is inferred because its history is absent.
Both explicitly mean discuss/debate. Other English senses are mostly inactive; Norwegian history is absent.

Domestic dog meaning explicitly overlaps, including Norwegian dog and female-dog senses. The English parent gloss a-person and selected female-dog counterpart miss it; secondary person/device senses should not dominate.
Both record home/dwelling and common haimaz ancestry. Selected English habitat-of-a-thing versus Norwegian origin/belonging is less direct than their ordinary dwelling correspondence.
English hurry describes a specific defensive-pressure event, not generic pressure; urgency and pressure can coincide but these entries do not establish general interchangeability.

Both explicitly record the airborne jumping action. Many English secondary meanings and the Norwegian mare homograph differ. Germanic jump history and Norse hoppa do not by themselves settle common ancestry.
Law/rule and correct regular order are associated, but bare rule is not an exact equivalent of arrangement. Norwegian law is obsolete/inactive; shared laga history is explicit.
Both explicitly identify the country Lesotho, with matching capital/location and recorded Sotho name; generic proper-name filtering would discard a valid pair.
Both identify a painting brush. The recorded compound versus Pinsel borrowing paths do not establish whole-word cognacy.
Healthy overlaps explicitly. English sound has many unrelated homographs and Norwegian frisk also means fresh, keen, or refreshing. Unequal Germanic roots do not settle common ancestry.
Both record statues and Latin statua through borrowing paths. English also has a statue-making verb and an inactive portrait sense.

The generic addition/supplement meaning overlaps, but the selected English dietary dosage sense is not disambiguated by the bare Norwegian supplement gloss. Latin/French history suggests a borrowing family without a full connecting path here.
Thatch can be straw used as roofing, but also rushes/leaves and other material; straw is not always thatch. Recorded roof-covering versus halmr history does not establish a common path.
Both identify winter and explicitly record wintruz ancestry. English metaphoric, verbal and name uses are additional meanings.
Both identify the working week. Recorded work-plus-week versus arbeid-plus-uke structures do not prove whole-compound inherited cognacy.
Both identify hemoglobin with recorded hemo/globin source components. Same scientific referent and shared constructed sources do not imply uninterrupted inherited transmission.
Chitin and an insect researcher differ; English entomolin is marked dated and rare/inactive. Shared entomon is only a component.
Division, portion, role, and partially are not a pair/couple/few or golf par. Association with two things does not establish equivalent senses.
Granada city/province and other named places are not Gran Canaria. Norwegian granka is explicitly its island abbreviation.
Both identify archdiocese. Recorded chief-plus-diocese versus arke-plus-stift constructions do not prove complete inherited component equivalence.
Killer meanings coincide, with English assassin generally narrower. Swedish baneman is archaic/inactive, so suitable current display differs from valid historical overlap.
A marijuana cigar and cigarette are related smoking products, not an exact shared sense. English blunt has many additional adjective, verb, and name uses; Swedish history is absent.
Brewing beer/liquor and coffee overlaps with common brewwanan ancestry. Swedish pier/bridge and English brow/name entries have different histories.
A technical-plan draughtsman belongs to the broader class of people who draw, but illustrator is not an exact universal equivalent. Game-piece and obsolete meanings are distinct.
Both explicitly record napkin. English diaper, scarf and inactive sanitary-napkin uses are additional meanings, not established Swedish correspondences.
Swedish native-edition mycology sense and its English pileus translation establish overlap omitted from the baseline target senses.
Physical putting is explicitly shared, but Swedish he is Northern/regional and also a pronoun. English abstract, financial and other senses do not all match.
Both record the rainbow phenomenon and Proto-Germanic regnabugo; English has additional uses.
Both record the Norse narrative sense and common saga source. English borrowing is narrower than Swedish fairy-tale/story uses; place-name homographs are separate.
The scraping verbs match with common skraponan ancestry, but the selected Swedish squeegee is a tool rather than the English action. Other noun and verb meanings differ.
Both mean summarize. Different recorded morphological bases do not prove independent origins, and Swedish also records conclude.
Demonstrative that is shared; English conjunction/relative uses and Swedish impersonal/article uses differ. Selected demonstrative versus placeholder functions are misaligned.
Both saved senses are marked inactive, and voting versus a suffragette remains action versus person. Historical tagging itself does not prove a word is unusable; report this filtering boundary.
The city or indigenous-person category and indigo colour/dye/plant do not share the saved senses.
The Pennsylvania borough and Swedish flat object/record meanings do not denote the same entity or concept.
Pain prevention or a protease inhibitor is not a religious opponent. Shared anti- does not relate the complete meanings.
Glutaric-acid-related and glutamine name different chemical concepts and grammatical categories. Similar scientific vocabulary is not equivalence.
Magnetic-moment units and magnetite mineral differ. A magnet-like component or topic does not establish exact meaning or full-word cognacy.
Musical group versus strap. The Norwegian sense is borrowed from English band; a deeper relation to binding cannot be settled from these records alone.
The settlement nouns share Old Norse byr. Current town/city versus village/hamlet meanings differ; Swedish town/city is marked obsolete. Verb and gust homographs are separate.
Both explicitly record effect/result. Latin effectus versus verka + suffix does not establish unrelated origins by itself.
Both mean field; borrowing histories involve German/Low German. Full ancestor-path verification remains separate.
A great-aunt is not any older woman. Norwegian family-friend senses can overlap Swedish older-woman address contextually; the aunt component history is shared, not the complete compound.
Both explicitly identify grasshopper, Swedish also locust. Both record grass-plus-hop composition; cross-language ancestry of each component is inferred rather than traced here.
Both mean lawn. Grass-like first components suggest partial family overlap, but plen and matta differ; whole-compound inherited cognacy is not documented.
The tickling verbs share Old Norse kitla and Germanic kitilonan; Norwegian wedge senses belong to another historical entry.
Road sign and emblem are different default objects; symbol/sign contexts might overlap and require additional lexical evidence.
Seashell overlaps explicitly with Swedish shell, and common skaljo history is recorded. Norwegian scale and Swedish peel/device-case meanings are additional.
Foam/froth overlaps explicitly. Swedish mouth-froth and verb uses and Norwegian lather differ in context; history is not connected here.
Search/seeking overlaps, but Swedish also records applicants/claimants. Similar search stems support inference; the Swedish complete ancestry path is absent.
Both descend through French tante, but the Swedish aunt sense is dated/inactive and its current older-woman use is broader than a kinship aunt.

Apostle overlaps explicitly, including religious and broader Swedish senses. Greek is recorded on one side and Old Swedish on the other; full common-source borrowing path is inferred, not fully recorded.
A fund and a font are different concepts. Only Norwegian historical evidence is recorded.
Conifer heartwood and ore/urban district/military field differ in saved modern meaning despite shared malmaz ancestry.
Saving is an action; a money saver is an agent. Swedish records spara plus agent suffix, but the cross-language historical link is inferred.
Responsibility and being responsible are related but different grammatical meanings. Swedish explicitly derives the verb from ansvar; the whole cross-language history needs a further link.
Adjective mysterious versus adverb mysteriously; useful grammatical comparison but not interchangeable forms or evidence of historical narrowing.
The spherical ball and Swedish penis/testicle/buttock/balcony senses differ, despite explicit common balluz ancestry. The Norwegian dance homograph has another origin.
Very drunk and dare are distinct senses and parts of speech. Swedish historical derivation does not establish Norwegian history.
Both mean hello, Swedish marked colloquial with a tentative blend history. A complete cross-language borrowing link is not recorded.
The Moselle river and Moses are explicitly different named entities; names should be assessed by identity rather than generic category similarity.
A single stimulus is explicitly recorded in Norwegian despite the stimuli form; automatic singular/plural rejection would be wrong. Norwegian collective and dope uses also occur; history is inferred.
Fox species versus Bengal region. Bengal+fox composition explains the shared component, not whole-word equivalence.
